cases.summary: Upload a PDF or a photo of a document; Claude classifies it, extracts the fields into a schema, a non-AI check validates the numbers, one repair attempt runs if they do not add up, and a person approves before anything is written to the database.
how: LangGraph pipeline: load → classify → extract → validate → (one repair loop) → review queue.
Claude's native PDF and vision input, so there is no separate OCR service.
Cross-field validation is plain code, not an LLM: cheap and deterministic.
At most three LLM calls per document: classify, extract and an optional repair.
A review queue shows the document next to the extracted fields; Approve & Commit writes the rows in one transaction.

cases.summary: An Airflow-orchestrated data platform that pulls SEC filings, prices and news every day, lands them in a 14-table DuckDB warehouse, scores each ticker from −100 to +100, and lets a Claude agent query it all through an MCP server.
how: Daily Airflow DAGs extract from SEC EDGAR, Yahoo Finance and Alpha Vantage.
Three tiers: raw Parquet, a 14-table DuckDB warehouse, and derived scores in their own partition.
Idempotent loads: appends dedupe on a declared primary key, so a re-run costs nothing.
A five-module scoring model blends price signals, EPS prediction, financial health and qualitative signals into one score.
An MCP server exposes named DuckDB queries as tools; a Claude agent (LangGraph) answers questions about the portfolio.

cases.summary: An email agent that reads inbound messages, sorts real leads from spam and support, extracts the lead's details, routes it to the right team using an editable rules table, and drafts a proposal document — then waits for a person before anything is sent.
how: A six-node LangGraph graph: it classifies the email, extracts the lead, routes it, drafts the proposal and hands it over.
Routing follows a keyword rules table the team can edit; Claude only breaks ties.
Proposals are generated as Word documents with python-docx.
At most four Claude calls per lead email.
Every run has a node-by-node trace, so you can see why a lead went where it did.

cases.summary: Point it at a folder of photos and it groups them by who is in them: SigLIP image embeddings and InsightFace face embeddings are clustered by a consensus vote across six thresholds, giving stable identity labels with no retraining, no labels and no fixed number of clusters.
how: Global image embeddings from SigLIP (google/siglip-so400m-patch14-384), batched and GPU-accelerated when available.
Face detection and face embeddings from InsightFace (buffalo_l).
Ensemble and consensus clustering across six thresholds, so identities stay stable on noisy photo sets.
Results are written into browsable folders and zipped.

cases.summary: A reference implementation of a four-agent system: a controller that proposes new ventures, a sandboxed code builder, capped-budget child agents, and a profit-blind ethics auditor that can veto the other three.
how: Mother agent: a stateful LangGraph controller that manages cash flow across three pots.
Code builder: stateless, generating tools inside a gVisor sandbox.
Ethics auditor: profit-blind, with a frozen prompt, and the power to veto.
Child agents: one per venture, each with a capped budget.
Frozen-config integrity: changing a protected file trips an alarm unless its hash is re-signed; an operator kill switch works over email.

cases.summary: A retrieval-augmented (RAG) app for getting up to speed on an unfamiliar codebase: ingest a repository, ask questions in plain English, and get answers grounded in the code with clickable file:line citations. When the code does not answer the question, it says so instead of guessing.
how: Ingests a local folder or a public GitHub repo, chunked with a line-window chunker.
Two retrieval modes: Postgres full-text search, or voyage-code-3 embeddings with pgvector.
A LangGraph flow rewrites the question, grades the retrieved chunks, then answers with citations.
At most three Claude calls per question.
An explicit 'not found' path, and every retrieved chunk and grade visible in the UI.

faqs: How much does a website for a small business cost?
With me, a one-page site starts at $200. Larger business sites, Shopify stores and custom stores cost more; you get one fixed price after a free 20-minute audit, before any work starts.
How much does an AI automation for a small business cost?

A single automation starts at $400, for example turning inquiries into drafted quotes. A bundle of three, or a custom AI agent for a bigger workflow, is quoted as one fixed price after the free audit.
How much does it cost to set up an AI assistant like Claude for my business?

A Claude for Small Business setup starts at $250 for one person: connected to the tools you already use, a few workflows tuned to your work, and a walkthrough. Team setups for 2 to 10 people are quoted after the audit.
Will an AI send messages to my customers without me?
No. Everything I build drafts first and waits: nothing goes to a customer until a person presses Approve.
Who owns the website, the data and the accounts?
You do. Software subscriptions are in your name and paid by you directly, systems run on accounts or machines you own, and you keep everything if we stop working together.
How do payments work?
A fixed quote, 50% up front and 50% on delivery, when it is live and you are happy with it.
What happens after it is delivered?
Two months of support are included: fixes and small changes, up to 5 hours a month. After that, $30 an hour if you need me.
Do you work with businesses in the US?
Yes. I am based in Lahore, Pakistan and work remotely with businesses in the US and worldwide; calls are booked for US mornings, which are my evenings.
Who is behind this?

Saad Waseem, an independent software engineer. I am the lead developer of AI Reports at Maiden Century, where Claude agents run over 100GB+ of financial data in production, and my demo projects are public on GitHub.
How do I start?
Book a free 20-minute audit. We talk through what is slowing the business down, and you get a fixed quote for the fix.
